Among 4662 laboratory-confirmed admissions, 67.2% were due to SARS-CoV-2 and 32.8% to influenza. Infants accounted for one-third to nearly half of SARS-CoV-2 admissions, while toddlers and school-aged children were more frequently hospitalized with influenza. Fever, cough and rhinitis were common in both infections, but fever was less frequent during the Omicron wave and the COVID period for influenza. Anosmia occurred only with SARS-CoV-2, whereas acute respiratory distress syndrome and lobar pneumonia (up to 20%) were recorded only among influenza cases. ICU admissions were higher for influenza (10.5–11.8%) than for SARS-CoV-2 (5.0–10.3%), and antibiotic use was greater in influenza (40.7%). Underlying neurological, cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were independently associated with severe disease for both viruses. The authors conclude that influenza in hospitalized children is associated with more severe outcomes than SARS-CoV-2 and recommend broader pediatric influenza vaccination and ongoing surveillance.
